body:
The artistic culture of the Harappans

The Mature Harappan Civilisation flourished approximately between 2600 BCE and 1900 BCE. Its artistic remains include stone sculptures, metal figurines, terracotta objects, seals, pottery, beads and ornaments.

Harappan art is especially important because it demonstrates skill in working with different materials. The surviving objects also provide evidence of dress, ornaments, craft production, commercial exchange and visual representation.

Major urban sites include Harappa and Mohenjo-daro in present-day Pakistan, along with Lothal and Dholavira in Gujarat and several other settlements in northwestern India.

Important sculptures and artefacts

ArtefactMaterialSiteIdentifying features
Male torsoRed sandstoneHarappaCarefully modelled body with sockets for attaching the head and arms
Bearded male bustSteatiteMohenjo-daroShawl with trefoil designs, carefully rendered facial features
Dancing GirlCopper alloy, commonly described as bronzeMohenjo-daroSmall standing female figure with numerous bangles and one hand resting on the hip
Female figurinesTerracottaVarious Harappan sitesElaborate head ornaments and simplified modelling
Animal sealsUsually steatiteVarious Harappan sitesAnimal motifs and signs of the undeciphered Harappan script

The Dancing Girl

The famous Dancing Girl from Mohenjo-daro is a small metal figure approximately 10.5 cm high. One arm has numerous bangles, and the other hand rests on the hip. Its pose and confident modelling demonstrate the metalworker's ability to represent the human body in three dimensions.

Its modern title is descriptive. The figure does not prove the existence of a particular dance tradition or establish the occupation of the person represented.

The bearded male figure

A stone bust from Mohenjo-daro depicts a bearded man wearing a shawl decorated with trefoil motifs. The figure is popularly called the Priest-King.

The name is a modern interpretation rather than a confirmed Harappan title. Archaeological evidence does not establish that this person was either a priest or a king.

Terracotta figurines

Terracotta means clay that has been shaped and fired to make it hard. Harappan craftsmen produced human figurines, animals, miniature carts, rattles and other small objects.

Some female figurines with elaborate headgear have traditionally been described as Mother Goddess figures. However, their religious identification is not certain. Similar-looking objects could have served different purposes in different contexts.

Harappan seals and iconography

Harappan seals were often made of steatite, a comparatively soft stone suitable for carving. They commonly carry animal figures, including the so-called unicorn, along with signs of the undeciphered Harappan script.

Seals could be pressed into clay sealings attached to packages or containers. An intact sealing could help identify the sender and indicate whether a package had been opened during transport.

One well-known seal from Mohenjo-daro depicts a seated central figure surrounded by animals. It is frequently called the Pashupati Seal. Some interpretations associate it with an early form of Shiva, but that identification is not established.

Metal casting and the lost-wax process

Harappan craftsmen used the lost-wax technique to produce metal figures. A model was prepared in wax, covered with a suitable mould material and heated so that the wax could escape. Molten metal was then introduced into the cavity. After cooling, the mould was removed to reveal the casting.

The method allowed artists to create three-dimensional human and animal figures. Related lost-wax traditions continued in later Indian metal sculpture.

Gujarat's contribution

Lothal was an important Harappan centre for bead production. Carnelian was obtained from sources in the Gujarat region, including the Bharuch area. Copper animal figures, including a dog and a bird, have been reported from Lothal.

Dholavira demonstrates the use of stone in Harappan construction, alongside evidence of urban organisation and water-management structures. These Gujarat sites show that Harappan artistic and technical traditions extended far beyond the Indus River valley itself.

Prelims focus

  • Mature Harappan Civilisation: approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
  • Dancing Girl: copper-alloy figure from Mohenjo-daro.
  • Bearded male bust: steatite, Mohenjo-daro; traditionally called Priest-King.
  • Male torso: red sandstone, Harappa.
  • Harappan seals commonly used steatite; their script remains undeciphered.
  • Trap: Neither the Priest-King title nor the Shiva interpretation of the Pashupati Seal is securely established.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 2, 'Arts of the Indus Valley', printed pp. 9–17; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class XII, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', especially sections on chronology, craft production, seals and script; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 7, 'Indian Bronze Sculpture', printed p. 103.]

title: Harappan Sculpture and Artistic Traditions of the Indus Civilisation

body:
The development of Mauryan stone art

The Mauryan Empire emerged in the 4th century BCE. During the reign of Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, monumental stone pillars, animal capitals and rock-cut works became important expressions of royal patronage and craftsmanship.

One characteristic of major Mauryan stone sculptures is their remarkably smooth, polished surface. This finish is often called Mauryan polish.

The period also witnessed artistic activity outside direct royal patronage, including large representations of yakshas and yakshis associated with widespread local beliefs.

Ashokan pillars

Ashokan pillars were generally carved from large, single pieces of stone. Their shafts demonstrate the ability of sculptors to produce tall, accurately shaped and polished stone forms.

The pillars were not merely decorative. Several carried inscriptions communicating Ashoka's policies and principles of dhamma.

Animal capitals included figures of lions, bulls and elephants. Important examples of Ashokan pillar capitals have been found at Sarnath, Rampurva, Sankisa and other sites.

The Sarnath Lion Capital

The Sarnath Lion Capital, associated with Ashoka, is among the most recognised sculptures of ancient India. The original capital is preserved at the Archaeological Museum, Sarnath.

Its most important elements include:

  • 4 lions: Seated back to back, facing different directions.
  • Circular abacus: A supporting drum decorated with animal figures.
  • 4 animals: An elephant, horse, bull and lion.
  • Dharmachakras: Wheels represented between the animal figures; each has 24 spokes.
  • Inverted lotus base: A bell-shaped lotus supporting the abacus.

The original composition also included a large crowning wheel, now damaged. Its imagery is associated with Dhammachakrapravartana, the Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath.

Relationship with India's State Emblem

India's State Emblem is an adaptation of the Sarnath Lion Capital. It does not reproduce every component of the original monument.

In the two-dimensional representation, 3 lions are visible, although the original capital contains 4 lions. The adopted emblem does not include the original inverted lotus base or the broken crowning wheel. The motto Satyameva Jayate, taken from the Mundaka Upanishad, forms part of the modern State Emblem and was not an inscription on the original sculpted capital.

Original sculpture: 4 lions and an inverted lotus base. Modern State Emblem: an adaptation in which 3 lions are visible from the front.

Yaksha and yakshi sculptures

Yakshas and yakshis were figures associated with local religious and protective traditions. Large stone representations were produced in places such as Mathura, Patna and Vidisha.

These figures often have substantial bodies, powerful postures and prominently modelled physical features. Their scale differs from the smaller objects commonly associated with earlier Harappan art.

The polished sandstone Chauri-Bearer Yakshi from Didarganj, Patna is frequently discussed in the context of Mauryan sculptural characteristics. Its smooth surface and carefully modelled body are especially notable, although its precise dating has been debated.

Rock-cut sculpture and caves

At Dhauli in Odisha, a rock-cut elephant is associated with an Ashokan inscription. The animal emerges from the natural rock surface, demonstrating a different approach from a free-standing pillar capital.

The Barabar Hills in Bihar contain early rock-cut caves. The entrance of the Lomas Rishi Cave is distinguished by a semicircular chaitya arch and sculpted elephants. These caves are associated with the Ajivika sect, which must be distinguished from Buddhism.

Why Mauryan sculpture matters

Mauryan art brings together monumental scale, refined stone finishing, animal representation and the use of inscriptions. It also provides important background for understanding later Buddhist sculptural programmes and the increasing decoration of stupas.

Prelims focus

  • Ashokan pillar sculpture is associated with the 3rd century BCE.
  • The Sarnath Lion Capital has 4 lions and 4 animal motifs on its abacus.
  • The dharma wheels on the Sarnath abacus have 24 spokes.
  • Mauryan sculpture is noted for highly polished stone surfaces.
  • Lomas Rishi Cave is in the Barabar Hills of Bihar and is associated with the Ajivikas.
  • Trap: The original Sarnath capital and the adopted State Emblem are not identical compositions.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 3, 'Arts of the Mauryan Period', printed pp. 19–25; Archaeological Museum, Sarnath, 'Capital of Ashokan Pillar', accession no. 355, consulted 23 November 2026; Government of India, official State Emblem description, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The original Sarnath capital has 4 lions, an animal-decorated abacus and an inverted lotus base.

title: Mauryan Sculpture: Polished Pillars, Lion Capital and Monumental Figures

body:
Why Buddhist stupas were built

A stupa is a mound-like structure associated with the preservation and veneration of relics or other sacred associations. Stupas became important monuments in Buddhist religious life.

The practice of constructing stupas existed before the mature development of Buddhist sculpture. During and after the Mauryan period, stupas increasingly acquired stone railings, gateways and carved narrative panels.

The Great Stupa at Sanchi began as a brick structure associated with Ashoka. Later additions transformed it into a much more elaborate stone monument.

Principal parts of a stupa

  • Anda: The hemispherical mound.
  • Harmika: A square enclosure above the mound.
  • Yashti: The upright mast rising from the upper part of the stupa.
  • Chhatra: An umbrella-like element associated with the mast.
  • Vedika: A railing separating the sacred area from its surroundings.
  • Torana: A gateway, often richly decorated with sculpture.
  • Pradakshinapatha: A path used for clockwise circumambulation around the monument.

Bharhut: Early narrative relief sculpture

Bharhut is located in Madhya Pradesh. Its early Buddhist sculptural remains are especially associated with the 2nd–1st centuries BCE.

Bharhut reliefs are generally comparatively shallow. Figures remain close to the background surface, and the forms can appear more rigid and linear than in later sculpture.

The railings contain representations of Jataka stories, which recount previous births of the Buddha, as well as episodes associated with his life.

Important examples include the Ruru Jataka, involving a compassionate deer, and the scene of Queen Maya's dream, represented through an elephant approaching the reclining queen.

Sanchi: Fuller forms and elaborate gateways

Sanchi is also in Madhya Pradesh. Its Great Stupa is particularly famous for 4 richly sculpted gateways, known as toranas.

The sculptural figures at Sanchi show greater projection, more natural postures and more elaborate narrative compositions than many earlier Bharhut reliefs.

The decorated gateways depict Jataka stories, events associated with the Buddha and a variety of human, animal and symbolic subjects.

Shalabhanjika figures, commonly represented as women holding tree branches, are important ornamental motifs in the sculptural programme.

Amaravati: Dynamic sculptural compositions

Amaravati in present-day Andhra Pradesh became a major centre of Buddhist sculpture. Its great stupa reached an important phase of artistic development during the 1st–2nd centuries CE.

Amaravati reliefs are distinguished by slender human figures, active movement, elaborate overlapping compositions and greater complexity in narrative scenes.

Many figures are represented in tribhanga, a posture in which the body bends at 3 points, creating a graceful sense of movement.

Stone slabs from the stupa's drum depict events from the Buddha's life and Jataka stories. Later phases also include anthropomorphic images of the Buddha.

Comparing the 3 centres

CentreRegionPrincipal sculptural characteristic
BharhutMadhya PradeshRelatively shallow, linear and restrained narrative relief
SanchiMadhya PradeshHigh-relief figures and elaborate carved gateways
AmaravatiAndhra PradeshSlender figures, dynamic movement and complex narrative arrangements

Symbolic and human representations of the Buddha

In many early Buddhist reliefs, the Buddha was represented through symbols rather than a human figure. An empty throne could indicate his presence or meditation, a Bodhi tree his enlightenment, a wheel his first sermon and a stupa his final passing away.

Such representation is often called aniconic representation. Later Buddhist sculpture increasingly included the Buddha in human form, although symbols continued to be used.

Who supported the sculptors?

Inscriptions record donations by rulers, merchants, artisans, guilds, monks, nuns and lay devotees. At Sanchi, inscriptions associate ivory workers with donations to the monument.

These records show that the construction and decoration of Buddhist monuments did not depend exclusively on royal patronage. Various sections of society contributed to religious and artistic activity.

Prelims focus

  • Bharhut and Sanchi are in Madhya Pradesh; Amaravati is in Andhra Pradesh.
  • Bharhut is associated with comparatively shallow narrative reliefs.
  • Sanchi's Great Stupa has 4 sculpted toranas.
  • Amaravati is known for movement, slender figures and elaborate narrative carving.
  • The dharma wheel is a prominent symbol of the Buddha's first sermon.
  • Trap: The early symbolic representation of the Buddha did not prevent later sculptors from creating human Buddha images.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 3, printed pp. 25–26, and Chapter 4, 'Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture', printed pp. 27–34 and 46–47; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class XII, Theme 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings', sections 'Stupas' and 'Sculpture', printed pp. 95–100.]
